dsprrr

Program LLMs in R instead of hand-tuning prompt strings.

Declare a task’s inputs and typed outputs once, swap reasoning and tool-use strategies without rewriting prompts, measure quality on labeled data, and let an optimizer fit instructions and examples to your metric. Built on ellmer and inspired by DSPy.

Get started How dsprrr works Coming from DSPy? →

Why program instead of prompt?

A hand-written prompt mixes three fragile things into one string: what you want, how to coax a particular model, and which examples to show. dsprrr keeps them separate so you can test, compare, and optimize LLM features like any other R code.

Hand-tuned prompt 

# Task and wording tangled in one string
chat$chat(paste(
  "Route this ticket. Return urgency",
  "(low/high) and team. Ticket:", ticket
))
  • Free-text output you have to parse by hand
  • Hard to test across rows or compare versions
  • Breaks quietly when you change models

Declarative dsprrr program 

sig <- signature(
  "ticket -> urgency: enum('low', 'high')"
)
router <- chain_of_thought(sig) |>
  compile(
    BootstrapFewShot(metric = metric),
    trainset = train
  )
  • Typed R list returned via structured schemas
  • Swap strategies or chain steps in one line
  • Measure with evaluate(), re-compile for any model

If you have a one-off prompt that already works and no data to measure it against, plain ellmer is enough. dsprrr earns its keep once an LLM call becomes a repeatable workflow you need to measure, compose, or port across models.

The R modeling mental model

If you have ever fit a model in R, you already know the loop:

1. Declare

signature()

Like y ~ x

State inputs, typed outputs, and task intent without writing prompt plumbing.

2. Build

module()

Like a model spec

Choose direct prediction, chain-of-thought, ReAct tools, or %>>% pipelines.

3. Measure

evaluate()

Like yardstick

Score predictions across a data frame and inspect prompts, traces, and cost.

4. Optimize

compile()

Like fit()

Search instructions and few-shot demos on training data to raise your metric.

How the pieces fit

One support-ticket workflow from declaration to a saved, compiled program:

01

Signatures

Declare the contract. Put inputs on the left of ->, typed outputs on the right, and optional instructions. dsprrr builds the prompt and JSON schema from this, so results arrive as typed R values ready for a data frame.

How dsprrr works →

library(dsprrr)

sig <- signature(
  "ticket -> urgency: enum('low', 'high'), team: string",
  instructions = "Route a support ticket."
)

02

Modules

Swap how it thinks. The same signature can run as one structured call, with step-by-step reasoning first, or in a tool-calling loop. Run any module on one input with run() or over a data frame with run_dataset().

Choose a module type →

chat <- ellmer::chat_openai(model = "gpt-6-luna")

router <- module(sig)                # one call
router_cot <- chain_of_thought(sig)  # reason first

lookup <- ellmer::tool(
  function(q) "Duplicate charges go to billing.",
  description = "Look up routing policy",
  arguments = list(q = ellmer::type_string())
)
router_agent <- react(sig, tools = list(lookup))

run(router, ticket = "Charged twice!", .llm = chat)

03

Pipelines

Compose multi-step programs. Chain modules with %>>% or wire inputs explicitly with pipeline() and step(). A pipeline is itself a module, so run(), evaluate(), and compile() work across all steps together.

Chain modules into pipelines →

draft <- module(signature(
  "urgency, team -> reply",
  instructions = "Write a brief acknowledgment."
))

# Outputs connect to matching inputs by name
triage <- module(sig) %>>% draft

run(triage, ticket = "Charged twice!", .llm = chat)

04

Metrics & evaluation

Measure instead of eyeballing. Split your labeled rows, run the module over the validation set, and score every prediction. Inspect misses, prompts (get_last_prompt()), traces (summarize_traces()), and spend (session_cost()).

Metrics and evaluation →

tickets <- tibble::tribble(
  ~ticket,                       ~urgency, ~team,
  "Charged twice for my order",  "high",   "billing",
  "Change my profile photo?",    "low",    "account",
  "App deletes files on sync",   "high",   "technical",
  "Need last year's invoice",    "low",    "billing",
  "Unknown login on my account", "high",   "account",
  "Export fails in Safari",      "low",    "technical"
)

splits <- split_dataset(tickets, prop = 0.67, seed = 1)
metric <- metric_exact_match(field = "urgency")

baseline <- evaluate(
  router, splits$val, metric = metric, .llm = chat
)
baseline$mean_score

05

Optimizers & persistence

Fit prompts to your data. compile() returns a new module whose demos or instructions were chosen to raise your metric on training rows (BootstrapFewShot, MIPROv2, GEPA, and more). Verify on held-out rows, then save with save_program(). Switch models? Swap chat and re-compile.

Compile and optimize →

optimizer <- BootstrapFewShot(
  metric = metric,
  max_bootstrapped_demos = 2L,
  max_labeled_demos = 0L
)

optimized <- router |>
  compile(optimizer, splits$train, .llm = chat)

evaluate(
  optimized, splits$val, metric, .llm = chat
)
save_program(optimized, "ticket_router.rds")

Works with your R stack

ellmer providers

Runs on any chat ellmer supports: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Ollama, Bedrock, and more.

vitals evaluation

Expose modules as vitals solvers and reuse vitals scorers directly as dsprrr metrics.

ragnar retrieval

Connect document stores to RAG modules and ReAct agents with ragnar_tool().

tidymodels

Tune LLM parameters alongside workflows with the llm_predict() parsnip spec.

pins & targets

Version compiled configs with pin_module_config() and orchestrate batch runs.

Caching, async & traces

Built-in memory and disk cache, run_async(), run_stream(), and token/cost logs.

Installation

Install the released version from CRAN:

install.packages("dsprrr")

Or install the development version from GitHub:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("JamesHWade/dsprrr")

Set a provider API key in your .Renviron (for example OPENAI_API_KEY or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY), then run dsprrr_sitrep() to verify your setup. Installing from source requires a C compiler (Rtools on Windows, Xcode Command Line Tools on macOS, or your Linux distribution’s build tools); the compiled helper preserves exact filesystem identities for safe persistence.

Experimental features: rlm_module() lets a model explore a large R object by writing code (How RLM works), flex() lets GEPA rewrite a whole program (Flex), with_decisions() and ReAnchor() calibrate decision thresholds (Calibrated decisions), and Omni() and the agentic harnesses compose optimizers (Omni, agentic harnesses).

dsprrr is experimental; the API may change. It is inspired by DSPy from Stanford NLP, builds on ellmer for model access, and bridges to vitals for evaluation.
